title: Vanilla-JS Interactive Kanban Board
tagline: Build a drag-and-drop task board with pure HTML, CSS, and JavaScript — no framework — so you understand the DOM, events, and state before any library does it for you.
summary: You'll build a fully working Kanban board (To Do / In Progress / Done) using only semantic HTML, modern CSS layout, and vanilla JavaScript. Cards can be created, edited, deleted, dragged between columns, and persisted to localStorage so the board survives a refresh. The point is fluency: by the end you'll know exactly what React's state and re-render model is replacing, because you'll have hand-written the DOM updates, event handling, and a single source of truth yourself.
scenario: Your team wants a lightweight internal task board with zero build step — something that can be dropped onto a static host and just works. You've been asked to prototype it with no dependencies so it loads instantly and is trivial to audit. The mandate is deliberately minimal: one HTML file, one stylesheet, one script, a single in-memory state object that is the source of truth, and the DOM rendered from that state. When the board misbehaves, you must be able to point at the exact line where state changed and the DOM failed to follow.
learningGoals: Model UI state as a single JavaScript object and render the DOM from it
Handle events with delegation instead of per-element listeners
Implement the native HTML Drag and Drop API correctly
Persist and rehydrate state with localStorage and JSON
Structure vanilla JS so it stays readable without a framework
skillsDemonstrated: Modern CSS layout with Flexbox and Grid
datasetDescription: There is no external dataset. The board's data is an in-memory array of card objects — each with an id, a title, a short description, and a column key ('todo' | 'doing' | 'done'). This array is the single source of truth; it is serialized to localStorage on every change and parsed back on load. A small seed set of 4-5 sample cards ships in the code so a first-time visitor sees a populated board.
architectureFlow: User action (add / edit / delete / drag) -> Update the state array (the single source of truth) -> Persist state to localStorage -> Re-render the affected column(s) from state -> DOM reflects state -> Repeat
repoStructure:
vanilla-kanban/
├── index.html          # semantic structure: header, 3 column sections
├── styles.css          # Flexbox columns, card styling, drag-over states
├── src/
│   ├── state.js        # the card array + load/save to localStorage
│   ├── render.js       # render board/columns/cards from state
│   ├── events.js       # delegated listeners: add, edit, delete, drag/drop
│   └── main.js         # wire it together on DOMContentLoaded
└── README.md           # screenshot/GIF + how state drives the DOM

milestones.title: Static structure & layout
milestones.goal: Lay out three columns with semantic HTML and CSS before any JavaScript.
tasks: Write semantic HTML: a header, and three <section> columns each with a heading and a card list
Use Flexbox (or Grid) to place the three columns side by side, responsive down to one column on narrow screens
Style a card component (title, description, delete button) with accessible contrast
Add a visible focus style for all interactive elements
acceptanceCriteria: The page is usable and readable with CSS only, no JS yet
Layout reflows to a single column below ~640px
HTML validates and uses landmarks (header, main, section)
hints: Give each column a data-column attribute ('todo'/'doing'/'done') — you'll read it later during drag/drop
Keep the card markup identical everywhere so one render function can produce it
milestones.deliverable: A static, styled, responsive three-column board with no interactivity.

milestones.title: State-driven rendering
milestones.goal: Introduce a single state array and render the whole board from it.
tasks: Create state.js exporting the cards array and getState/setState helpers
Write a render(state) function that clears and repopulates each column from state
Call render() once on load with seed data
Never mutate the DOM directly outside render() — always change state then re-render
acceptanceCriteria: Changing the state array and calling render() updates the UI
No DOM node is created outside the render function
Cards appear in the correct column based on their column key
hints: Re-rendering an entire column on each change is fine at this scale — correctness first
Use element.replaceChildren(...) to clear a column cleanly
milestones.deliverable: A board rendered entirely from a state object.

milestones.title: Add, edit, delete via event delegation
milestones.goal: Mutate state through a single delegated listener, then persist it.
tasks: Attach one click listener on the board container and branch on event.target
Implement add-card (per column), edit-title (inline or prompt), and delete-card
After each mutation, save state to localStorage and re-render
Load persisted state on startup, falling back to the seed data
acceptanceCriteria: Adding, editing, and deleting all work and survive a page refresh
Only one or two listeners exist on the board, not one per card
Malformed/empty localStorage is handled without crashing
hints: Give each card a stable id (crypto.randomUUID()) so edits/deletes target the right one
Wrap JSON.parse in try/catch when reading localStorage
milestones.deliverable: A persistent board with full create/edit/delete.

milestones.title: Drag and drop between columns
milestones.goal: Move cards across columns with the native Drag and Drop API, updating state.
tasks: Make cards draggable and set the card id in the dataTransfer payload on dragstart
Handle dragover/drop on each column, reading the target column's data attribute
On drop, update the dragged card's column in state, persist, and re-render
Add a clear drag-over visual state on the target column
acceptanceCriteria: A card can be dragged to any column and stays there after refresh
The target column shows a visible drop affordance while dragging over it
State remains the single source of truth — the card's column key is what changed
hints: Call event.preventDefault() in dragover or drop will never fire
Don't move DOM nodes by hand on drop — change state and let render() place the card
milestones.deliverable: A complete, persistent, drag-and-drop Kanban board in vanilla JS.

productionChecklist: Keyboard accessibility: cards and buttons are focusable and operable without a mouse
ARIA: columns labelled, drag alternative provided (e.g. a move menu) for non-drag users
No console errors; graceful handling of empty/corrupt localStorage
README with a GIF of drag-and-drop and a note on the state->DOM model
Code split into small modules with no global leakage
stretchGoals: Add per-column card counts and a filter/search box
Add undo for the last action
Animate card movement with the FLIP technique
Add a dark mode with a CSS custom-property theme
Export/import the board as JSON
portfolioTips: This is your fundamentals credibility anchor: it proves you understand the DOM, events, and state without hiding behind a framework. Lead the README with the state->persist->render diagram and a short GIF of a card being dragged across columns so a reviewer instantly sees it working. Call out the deliberate no-dependency constraint and the single-source-of-truth model, because those are exactly the maturity signals interviewers probe. On your resume phrase it as an outcome: 'Built a persistent drag-and-drop Kanban board in vanilla JS with a single-source-of-truth state model and delegated event handling.' Note that it deploys to any static host with zero build step.

title: React Weather Dashboard with Data Fetching
tagline: Build a typed React dashboard that fetches, caches, and displays live data with proper loading, error, and empty states — the everyday job of a frontend engineer.
summary: You'll build a React + TypeScript weather dashboard: search a city, fetch current conditions and a multi-day forecast from a public API, and render it with first-class loading, error, and empty states. You'll manage async state with a custom hook, debounce the search, cache results so re-searching a city is instant, and handle the failure paths real apps must handle. This is the transferable pattern behind almost every product screen — search, fetch, cache, render the three states — done properly instead of with a naked useEffect that ignores errors.
scenario: You've joined a team that keeps shipping screens where the loading spinner never stops on error and a failed request shows a blank page. You've been asked to build a reference implementation of 'the right way' to fetch and display remote data in React: a small weather dashboard that a teammate can read as the canonical example of async state, caching, and state handling. It must never leave the user staring at a spinner with no explanation, and must not refetch data it already has.
learningGoals: Fetch data in React without race conditions or stale updates
Model the four async states explicitly: idle, loading, success, error
Extract data fetching into a reusable typed custom hook
Debounce user input and cache responses in memory
Type API responses with TypeScript so the UI can't read fields that don't exist
skillsDemonstrated: Async state handling and cancellation with AbortController
Loading / error / empty / success UI states
datasetDescription: Data comes from a free public weather API such as Open-Meteo (no key required) or a similar service. You'll type two shapes: a geocoding response (city name -> latitude/longitude/label) and a forecast response (current temperature, conditions, and an array of daily entries with date, min/max temp, and a weather code). A small local map translates numeric weather codes to human labels and icons. Mock JSON fixtures of both responses are kept for tests and offline development.
architectureFlow: User types a city -> Debounced search input -> useWeather hook fires geocode request (AbortController cancels the previous one) -> Coordinates -> Forecast request -> Response typed & normalized -> Cache by city key -> Render success | show loading skeleton | show error with retry | show empty prompt
repoStructure:
weather-dashboard/
├── index.html
├── src/
│   ├── main.tsx
│   ├── App.tsx
│   ├── components/
│   │   ├── SearchBar.tsx        # debounced controlled input
│   │   ├── CurrentWeather.tsx   # current conditions card
│   │   ├── Forecast.tsx         # multi-day grid
│   │   └── StateViews.tsx       # Loading / Error / Empty components
│   ├── hooks/
│   │   └── useWeather.ts        # the fetch+cache+state hook
│   ├── lib/
│   │   ├── api.ts               # typed fetch wrappers
│   │   └── weatherCodes.ts      # code -> label/icon map
│   └── types.ts                 # GeocodeResult, Forecast, etc.
├── fixtures/                    # sample API responses for tests
└── README.md

milestones.title: Typed API layer
milestones.goal: Define the data types and typed fetch wrappers before touching the UI.
tasks: Write TypeScript interfaces for the geocode and forecast responses
Write api.ts functions that fetch and return those typed shapes
Normalize the raw API response into a clean internal model the UI will consume
Add fixtures (sample JSON) so you can develop without hitting the network
acceptanceCriteria: No use of any in the API layer
A single normalize function converts raw responses to the internal model
Functions reject/throw on non-OK HTTP responses
hints: Keep the raw API type and your internal type separate — normalize between them
Return a typed Promise so the hook that calls it is fully typed
milestones.deliverable: A typed, tested API module that returns clean data.

milestones.title: The useWeather hook
milestones.goal: Encapsulate fetching and the four async states in one reusable hook.
tasks: Model state as a discriminated union: { status: 'idle' | 'loading' | 'success' | 'error', ... }
Fetch inside the hook and update state through each phase
Cancel the previous request with AbortController when the city changes
Guard against setting state after unmount
acceptanceCriteria: Rapidly changing the city never shows results for a stale request
The hook exposes a single typed state value plus a retry function
No 'setState after unmount' warnings in the console
hints: A discriminated union makes impossible states impossible — lean on it
Return an AbortController's signal into fetch and abort in the effect cleanup

milestones.title: Render all four states
milestones.goal: Build the UI for loading, error, empty, and success — not just the happy path.
tasks: Build a skeleton/loading view, an error view with a retry button, and an empty prompt
Render current conditions and a multi-day forecast grid on success
Switch views off the hook's status field, never off truthiness of data
Map weather codes to labels and icons
acceptanceCriteria: Turning off the network shows the error state with a working retry, not a blank page
Before any search, the user sees a helpful empty prompt
Each state is a distinct, intentional view
hints: A switch on status keeps the render readable and exhaustive
Test the error path by pointing the API at a bad URL
milestones.deliverable: A dashboard that handles every state gracefully.

milestones.title: Debounce & cache
milestones.goal: Make search feel instant and stop refetching data you already have.
tasks: Debounce the search input so requests fire only after the user pauses
Cache forecast results in memory keyed by city
Serve cached results immediately and skip the network on repeat searches
Show a subtle 'updated just now / from cache' indicator
acceptanceCriteria: Typing quickly fires one request, not one per keystroke
Re-searching a previously loaded city renders instantly with no network call
Cache does not leak stale data across unrelated cities
hints: A Map<string, Forecast> in a ref or module scope is enough for in-memory cache
Debounce ~300ms is a good default; make it a constant
milestones.deliverable: A fast, cached, debounced weather dashboard.

productionChecklist: All four async states are implemented and visually distinct
No race conditions — verified by rapid city switching
No any in the codebase; API data fully typed
Accessible: labelled search input, keyboard-operable, sensible focus order
Responsive layout from mobile to desktop
Empty and error states give the user a next action
README documents the fetch->cache->render pattern and links a live deploy
Deployed to a static host / Vercel with the API called client-side
stretchGoals: Persist the last-searched city and recent searches to localStorage
Add unit tests for the hook and normalize function with the fixtures
Add a unit toggle (C/F) driven by derived state, not a second fetch
Replace the hand-rolled cache with TanStack Query and compare
Add geolocation to load the user's local weather on first visit
portfolioTips: This project proves you can do the actual daily job of a frontend engineer: fetch remote data correctly. Reviewers and interviewers care far more about how you handle the error and loading states than the happy path, so lead your README with screenshots of all four states side by side. Call out the race-safety (AbortController), the discriminated-union state model, and the caching, because those are senior signals most candidates miss. Phrase it on your resume as an outcome: 'Built a typed React data dashboard with race-safe fetching, in-memory caching, debounced search, and first-class loading/error/empty states.' Mention it's deployed and calls the API client-side so it's reproducible with no backend.

title: Typed API Client Library (TypeScript)
tagline: Build a small, fully-typed API client with a declaration file — proving you can design types, not just annotate them.
summary: You'll build a reusable, strongly-typed API client in TypeScript: typed request/response models, a generic request() wrapper, runtime validation at the boundary, typed errors, and a published .d.ts so consumers get full IntelliSense. The goal is type design — using generics, unions, and utility types so the compiler catches misuse before runtime.
scenario: Your team keeps hand-writing fetch calls with any everywhere, so typos in field names ship to production. You've been asked to build the canonical typed client every feature will import: one place where endpoints, params, and responses are described once and enforced everywhere.
learningGoals: Design types (generics, unions, utility types), not just annotate values
Validate untrusted data at the boundary and narrow it to a typed model
Model success/error results with a discriminated union
Author and ship a .d.ts declaration file
Configure strict tsconfig and fix what it flags
datasetDescription: No external dataset. You target a public JSON API (e.g. a users/posts placeholder API) and model two or three resources with TypeScript interfaces, plus a set of fixtures for tests. The 'domain model' is your type layer: request configs, typed responses, and a discriminated Result<T> union.
architectureFlow: Caller invokes a typed method -> request<T>(config) builds the URL & options -> fetch -> validate the JSON at the boundary -> narrow to T -> return Result<T> = { ok: true, data: T } | { ok: false, error } -> caller handles both branches with the compiler's help
repoStructure:
typed-api-client/
├── src/
│   ├── client.ts        # request<T>() core + typed methods
│   ├── types.ts         # resource models, Result<T> union
│   ├── validate.ts      # boundary validation -> typed model
│   └── index.ts         # public exports
├── dist/                # build output incl. .d.ts
├── fixtures/
└── tsconfig.json        # strict: true

milestones.title: Model the domain with types
milestones.goal: Describe resources and a Result union before any fetch code.
tasks: Write interfaces for 2-3 resources (e.g. User, Post).
Define Result<T> as a discriminated union of success and error.
Enable strict mode in tsconfig and fix errors.
Add fixtures matching each resource shape.
acceptanceCriteria: No any anywhere.
Result<T> forces callers to handle both branches.
tsconfig has strict: true.
hints: A generic request<T>() with typed methods (getUser, listPosts).
Every response is validated then narrowed to its type.
Non-OK responses become a typed error Result, not a throw.
Callers can't access .data without checking ok first.
deliverable: A typed request core returning Result<T>.

milestones.title: Generic request core
milestones.goal: Build request<T> and typed resource methods.
tasks: Implement request<T>(config): Promise<Result<T>>.
Add typed methods that call request<T> with the right T.
Validate JSON at the boundary and narrow to T.
Return a typed error Result on non-OK or invalid data.
acceptanceCriteria: Methods infer their return type from T.
Invalid data yields an error Result, never a wrong-typed success.
this-free, tree-shakeable functions.
hints: Wrap fetch; pass the expected type as T.
Validate with Zod or hand-written guards before returning data.

milestones.title: Ship types & docs
milestones.goal: Emit a .d.ts and document usage.
tasks: Configure the build to emit declarations.
Verify consumer IntelliSense in a scratch file.
Write a README with typed usage examples.
Add unit tests using the fixtures.
acceptanceCriteria: dist ships a .d.ts.
A consumer gets autocomplete and type errors on misuse.
Tests cover success + error + invalid-data paths.
hints: declaration: true in tsconfig.
Import from dist in a test file to confirm the public types.
deliverable: A published-shape typed library with declarations and tests.

stretchGoals: Add request cancellation (AbortController) typed through
Add a retry with typed backoff config
Generate types from an OpenAPI schema
Add branded types for IDs
portfolioTips: This is your TypeScript-depth proof. Reviewers can tell in seconds whether you design types or just sprinkle annotations. Lead the README with the Result<T> union and a screenshot of the compiler catching a bad field name. Phrase it as: 'Built a fully-typed API client with generic request handling, boundary validation, a discriminated Result type, and shipped .d.ts declarations.'

title: React Kanban with Drag-Drop & Global State
tagline: A real app with cross-component state, drag-and-drop, and persistence — the kind of build interviewers ask you to extend live.
summary: You'll build a Kanban board in React + TypeScript: columns and cards, drag-and-drop between columns, add/edit/delete, and a global store (Context+reducer or Zustand) as the single source of truth, persisted to localStorage. Emphasis on state architecture, derived state, and keeping re-renders scoped.
scenario: Product wants an internal task board. You're the frontend owner: design the state model so features (filters, labels, assignees) can be added without rewrites, and keep drag interactions smooth.
learningGoals: Design a normalized client state model
Choose and justify a state solution (Context+reducer vs a store)
Implement drag-and-drop with correct state updates
Scope re-renders with selectors/memoization
Persist and rehydrate app state safely
datasetDescription: No backend. State is a normalized store: { columns: {id -> {id, title, cardIds[]}}, cards: {id -> {id, title, ...}}, columnOrder: [] }. Seed data ships in code; the whole store persists to localStorage and rehydrates on load.
architectureFlow: UI event (add/move/edit) -> dispatch action / call store setter -> reducer produces next normalized state -> persist to localStorage -> selectors feed only the components that changed -> DOM updates
repoStructure:
react-kanban/
├── src/
│   ├── store/            # store + actions + selectors
│   ├── components/       # Board, Column, Card, CardEditor
│   ├── types.ts          # normalized state types
│   └── App.tsx
└── ...

Seed initial data.

No prop-drilling of the entire state.

milestones.goal: Move cards within and across columns via state.
tasks: Implement drag-and-drop (native or dnd-kit).
On drop, update card order/column in the store.
Reconcile order arrays, not DOM nodes.
Keep the dragged-over column visually indicated.

State (order arrays) is the source of truth, not the DOM.
Drop targets show affordance.

title: Real-Time Chat UI (streaming updates)
tagline: Handle a live stream of data with correct ordering, optimistic sends, and bounded rendering — the hard parts of real-time UIs.
summary: You'll build a chat UI that receives a live stream of messages (a mock WebSocket you control), sends optimistically, keeps scroll pinned to the latest, handles reconnection, and stays smooth as history grows. The focus is the real-time correctness problems: ordering, optimistic reconciliation, and not re-rendering thousands of messages.
scenario: You're building the chat surface for a support tool. Messages arrive continuously; users send while offline blips happen. It must feel instant and never lose or duplicate messages.
learningGoals: Consume a streaming source and update state correctly
Send optimistically and reconcile with the server ack
Keep scroll anchored to newest while allowing scroll-up
Handle reconnection and out-of-order/duplicate messages
Keep rendering bounded as history grows
datasetDescription: No real server. A mock 'socket' module emits messages on an interval and echoes sent messages after a delay (to simulate acks). Messages have id, author, text, and timestamp; the client keeps them in a Map/array keyed by id to dedup and order.
architectureFlow: Mock socket emits -> onMessage dedups by id & inserts in timestamp order -> state updates -> list renders (windowed) -> user sends -> optimistic message added with temp id -> ack replaces temp id with real id -> scroll pins to newest unless user scrolled up
repoStructure:
realtime-chat/
├── src/
│   ├── socket.ts         # mock socket: onMessage, send, reconnect
│   ├── useChat.ts        # state: messages, send, status
│   ├── components/       # MessageList, Composer, StatusBar
│   └── App.tsx
└── ...

milestones.title: Mock socket + receive
milestones.goal: Stream messages into ordered, deduped state.
tasks: Build a mock socket that emits messages on an interval.
Store messages keyed by id; dedup and keep timestamp order.
Render the message list.
Show a connection status indicator.
acceptanceCriteria: Duplicate ids never appear twice.
Messages stay in timestamp order even if they arrive out of order.
Status reflects connected/disconnected.
hints: Use a Map<id,msg> then a sorted view.
Ignore a message whose id already exists.
deliverable: A live, ordered, deduped message list.

milestones.title: Optimistic send
milestones.goal: Send instantly and reconcile on ack.
tasks: Add a composer; on send, insert an optimistic message with a temp id.
When the ack arrives, replace the temp id with the real one.
Mark pending messages visually until acked.
Handle send failure by flagging the message.
acceptanceCriteria: Sent messages appear instantly.
Ack replaces (not duplicates) the optimistic message.
Failures are visible and retryable.
hints: Track temp ids; match acks by a client token.
Don't insert twice when the ack echoes back.

milestones.title: Scroll + scale + reconnect
milestones.goal: Pin scroll, window the list, and recover.
tasks: Auto-scroll to newest unless the user scrolled up.
Window/virtualize the list as history grows.
Simulate a disconnect and reconnect, backfilling missed messages.
Keep memory bounded.
acceptanceCriteria: Scroll stays pinned to newest, but respects manual scroll-up.
Thousands of messages stay smooth.
After reconnect, no missing or duplicate messages.
hints: Track 'is at bottom' with IntersectionObserver.
On reconnect, request messages since the last seen id.
deliverable: A scalable, resilient real-time chat UI.

stretchGoals: Typing indicators & read receipts
Message grouping by author/time
Real WebSocket backend swap-in
Offline queue that flushes on reconnect
portfolioTips: Real-time is where most portfolios are thin, so this stands out. Lead with a GIF of streaming + optimistic send and a note on how you dedup/order and handle reconnect. Say: 'Built a real-time chat UI with optimistic sends, id-based dedup/ordering, scroll anchoring, windowing, and reconnect backfill.'

title: Capstone: Full-Stack Next.js Product (App Router)
tagline: Ship a real, deployed App-Router product with server actions, a caching strategy, and auth — the build you defend in a senior interview.
summary: The capstone ties the whole roadmap together: a deployed Next.js App Router application with Server Components, mutations via Server Actions, an explicit per-fragment caching/revalidation strategy, authentication with protected routes, and a written architecture doc. This is the end-to-end artifact that proves you can make production rendering, data, and auth decisions — not just build components.
scenario: You're the founding frontend engineer for a small product (pick one: a bookmarks manager, a job board, or a habit tracker). You own rendering strategy, data mutations, auth, performance, and the deploy. You must be able to defend every caching and rendering choice.
learningGoals: Choose rendering per route (static/ISR/dynamic/streamed) by data volatility
Mutate data with Server Actions and revalidate the right cache
Implement auth with protected routes and session handling
Optimize Core Web Vitals and ship to a real host
Document and defend the architecture
techStack: A DB or serverless store (or mocked BFF)
datasetDescription: A small domain of 2-3 entities (e.g. users + items + tags). Data lives in a lightweight DB or serverless KV, or a mocked backend-for-frontend if staying client-first. Product content is cacheable; user-specific and mutable data is fetched fresh or revalidated on write.
architectureFlow: Request -> App Router matches route -> Server Components render (cacheable content from Data Cache / ISR) -> dynamic & personalized parts stream via Suspense -> mutations go through Server Actions -> revalidateTag/Path purges affected caches -> auth middleware protects private routes -> CDN serves cacheable output
repoStructure:
nextjs-capstone/
├── app/
│   ├── (public)/         # static/ISR marketing + listings
│   ├── (app)/            # authed product area
│   ├── api/ or actions/  # server actions / route handlers
│   └── layout.tsx
├── lib/                  # data access, auth, caching helpers
├── middleware.ts         # route protection
└── ARCHITECTURE.md       # the doc you defend

milestones.title: Rendering & data plan
milestones.goal: Decide rendering per route before building.
tasks: List every route and classify its data (static/volatile/personalized).
Choose static/ISR/dynamic/streamed per route and write it down.
Set up data access in lib/.
Scaffold the App Router structure with route groups.
acceptanceCriteria: Each route has a documented rendering choice.
Static content is cacheable; personalized content is not route-cached.
ARCHITECTURE.md started.
hints: Partition by data volatility (see the caching visual).
Use route groups to separate public vs authed.
deliverable: A routed skeleton with a written rendering plan.

milestones.title: Server Actions & caching
milestones.goal: Implement mutations and correct revalidation.
tasks: Build create/update/delete as Server Actions.
Use useActionState/useFormStatus for pending + errors.
Call revalidateTag/revalidatePath so caches stay correct on write.
Add optimistic UI where it helps.
acceptanceCriteria: Mutations work and the UI reflects fresh data immediately.
Only the affected caches are purged on a write.
